description: Comprising 12 articles, this cluster examines the intersection of sustainability, luxury, marketing, and consumer behaviour. These studies collectively explore the dynamic relationship between high-end products and sustainable consumption. A recurrent theme within these studies is durability in high-end products as a catalyst for sustainable consumption, which is evident in the findings of Sun, Bellezza, and Paharia (2021), that accentuate the significance of product durability, showcasing that luxury goods characterised by their longevity and extended life cycles can contribute substantially to consumers' participation in sustainable consumption. It is reinforced by Karaosman et  al.  (2020), where real-world data affirms that high-end accessories can outshine mid-range products in sustainability metrics due to their prolonged usability. These findings by Karaosman et  al.  (2020) and Sun, Bellezza, and Paharia (2021) challenge the traditional view of luxury as inherently unsustainable due to perceived overconsumption, suggesting that a shift in consumer expectations can occur if durability is effectively communicated as an attribute of luxury. As highlighted earlier, sustainability has often been perceived as juxtaposed with compromise on other benefits owing to zero-sum heuristics (Newman, Gorlin, and Dhar  2014). Hence, accentuating the durability of luxury products can help redefine consumer expectations and attract environmentally conscious consumers. This extends Signalling Theory (Spence 1973) by suggesting that signalling durability may not only enhance luxury's exclusivity but also frame sustainability as a status symbol, positioning eco-conscious consumers as part of a desired group. Also, leveraging Kapferer's (2010) findings on the possibility of luxury being associated with sustainability through quality and identifying the right communication mechanisms for juxtaposing longevity as a luxury element could be an appealing area for study. Another common thread revolves around the intersection of sustainability and consumer perceptions. Research in this area (Blasi, Brigato, and Sedita 2020; Kong, Witmaier, and Ko 2021) has also explored the correlation between fashion and ecofriendliness perception, revealing that luxury brands exhibit a stronger alignment between these attributes than high and fast-fashion counterparts. This finding suggests a growing inclination to integrate environmental considerations as an integral part of the luxury brand identity and business strategy. These results challenge the existing belief by suggesting that sustainability may enhance rather than undermine luxury's exclusivity. Several studies (Cheah, Zainol, and Phau  2016; Turunen and Leipämaa-Leskinen 2015) contribute to understanding the influence of authenticity and ethical practices on consumer judgments of luxury products. These investigations demonstrate that consumers positively evaluate luxury items when associated with authentic country-of-origin (COO) ingredients and sustainable and ethical practices. Theoretically, this highlights the importance of examining how sustainability signalling can shape brand identity. Practically, luxury brands should integrate eco-friendly initiatives into their core strategies and brand messaging to attract eco-conscious consumers. This shaping of consumer perceptions of luxury offerings could be done by showcasing the interconnectedness of perceived authenticity, ethical sourcing, and sustainable practices. Setting flagship stores to communicate sustainability commitments for luxury products has been studied by Arrigo  (2018). This study emphasises how the design and management of physical retail spaces play a crucial role in conveying the dedication of luxury fashion brands to reinforce sustainable development and their sustainability initiatives. This calls for research exploring how the design of flagship stores influence consumer perceptions of sustainability, the effectiveness of different communication strategies within these stores, and the impact of flagship store's sustainability initiatives on overall brand reputation and consumer behaviour. There is also scope for measuring responses to different luxury offerings. For example, store expectations for a luxury durable could differ greatly from luxury fashion. With luxury fashion emerging as one of the motor themes in the 2015–2024 thematic map (Figure 8c), the role of stores gains significance in this context. In an environment that is increasingly evolving into omnichannel, this research can be extended to an online setup to explore how physical and digital environments contribute towards a unified sustainability narrative. In summary, the papers within this cluster provide a comprehensive understanding of sustainability in the luxury domain, highlighting the multifaceted relationships between durability, consumer perceptions, authenticity, and retail communication in pursuing more sustainable practices. The results indicate that the common belief of a paradoxical relationship between sustainability and luxury is unfounded. By focusing on product attributes/benefits such as durability and authenticity and choosing other attributes innovatively integrates sustainability and luxury.

This cluster consists of 12 studies dealing with topics ranging from organisational policies and leadership in luxury resorts to the adaptive responses of Michelin-starred chefs during crises. It also comprises intrinsic motivations shaping sustainable food experiences, tourists' preferences for green hotel attributes, the impact of social media on guests' perceptions of green practices, and challenges in aligning environmental beliefs with actual behaviour in the consumption of green hotel products. As depicted in the thematic map (Figure 8a,b), luxury hospitality has been a strong research area, with green hotels continuing to carry high density throughout the research period. Taking a different angle, Farooq et al. (2022) highlight the role of Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) in cultivating green creativity (GC) among employees in luxury resorts and hotels. The findings from this study show a positive association between GHRM and GC, affirming the significance of organisational policies and leadership in stimulating innovative responses to environmental challenges. Moreover, the mediating influence of Green Self-Efficacy is a crucial pathway through which GHRM impacts GC (Farooq et al. 2022). Their research contributes to theory by demonstrating how green leadership can drive innovation in luxury hospitality. It suggests that organisational culture may be more influential than individual beliefs in motivating sustainable practices. Researchers need to explore if this model would be effective in other luxury sectors like fashion or retail. Future research could also explore the long-term effects of GHRM practices on employee retention and job satisfaction in luxury hotels. Studies on crisis management and leveraging sustainability for the greater good emerged as a strong theme in the post2000 domain in shaping consumer preferences (Figure  8c). These studies collectively reveal a multifaceted approach luxury restaurants adopt, encompassing philanthropic activities, socially responsible business practices, and initiatives to enhance community and consumer well-being. Luxury hospitality brands' response to the COVID-19 crisis shows their ability to adapt and use the situation to strengthen their sustainability efforts. This adds to the resilience theory literature (Folke 2006) by illustrating how brands can not only recover but also improve by innovating. Future researchers could examine how these strategies might apply to brand management in other luxury sectors. A consistent theme emerges within sustainable food experiences in luxury gastronomy, highlighting the significance of chefs' perspectives. Batat  (2020) advocates for a comprehensive definition of sustainable luxury food experiences that incorporate functional and experiential aspects. The intrinsic motivations of Michelin-starred chefs, including plate, pleasure, and place considerations, contribute to a better comprehension of sustainability within the luxury gastronomy sector (Batat  2020). Related to this, the study of creative and resourceful thinking highlights how luxury gastronomy adapts and innovates during times of crisis (Batat 2021). While their research has mainly focused on chefs, consumers' views on sustainable food practices can be further explored. Studying whether consumer expectations match the sustainability efforts of luxury restaurants could further our understanding of consumer behaviour. Similarly, further studies could examine the role of consumer expectations in shaping adaptive strategies during times of crisis. It would also be useful to study consumers' perceptions of food ethics (promoting environmental sustainability, improving food well-being, investing in preservation of cultural heritage) while dining at luxury restaurants (Batat 2022). Amongst other related areas of research, exploring communication strategies for luxury restaurants, content (what to share) and medium (how to share), and the moderating role of individual consumer's consumption value would significantly contribute to literature. Chia-Jung and Pei-Chun  (2014) investigate tourists' preferences and willingness to pay for green hotel attributes in the Taiwanese market. The findings highlight tourists' preferences for luxury rooms and personal toiletries and their willingness to accept trade-offs, such as reduced service quality, in the pursuit of environmentally friendly options. The discerning role of the green consumption trait significantly influences tourists' choices, suggesting opportunities for targeted marketing strategies within luxury hotels (Chia-Jung and Pei-Chun  2014). This reveals a market segment willing to prioritise sustainability over traditional luxury attributes, demonstrating targeted marketing strategies. Examining the specific trade-offs consumers are willing to make for green attributes in hospitality could provide more precise marketing strategies. Investigating the impact of social media on shaping guests' perceptions of green practices reveals actionable directions for luxury hospitality (Lee, Jai, and Li 2016). The findings accentuate the positive response of guests when environmental initiatives are acknowledged, positioning social media as a potential educational tool and effective advertising platform. Using social media for sustainability communication can enhance guest engagement and brand perception. Studying the effectiveness of different types of social media content on consumer engagement could support targeted marketing in hospitality. However, challenges such as limited awareness and feedback mechanisms, signal areas for refinement in communication strategies (Lee, Jai, and Li 2016). Line and Hanks  (2016) focus on the disconnection between environmental beliefs and behaviours in the consumption of green hotel products. Their research findings underscore the challenges in translating consumers' environmental values into tangible actions within the luxury hotel sector. Exploring psychological barriers, such as concerns about perceived compromises in luxury, service quality, and comfort, that prevent consumers from acting on their environmental beliefs within the context of luxury hotels could provide valuable insights. Factors such as perceived luxury trade-offs and destination image influence consumers' attitudes towards green hotels, emphasising the nuanced nature of sustainable consumption behaviours (Line and Hanks 2016). From a destination marketing perspective, investigating how overall sustainable tourism destination image influences consumer preferences for luxury hotel attributes needs exploration.

The eight papers in this cluster provide compelling findings at the intersection of shared economy, CSR, and ethics within the luxury industry. Studies have highlighted the shifting dynamics of consumer behaviour in adopting a shared economy model for luxury fashion consumption, particularly among millennials (Jain and Mishra 2020; Pantano and Stylos 2020). Social projection value surfaces as a crucial predictor in this context, stressing the influence of social factors on luxury sharing economy decisions (Jain and Mishra 2020), which aligns with Social Identity theory (Tajfel 1978). This theory suggests that individuals' consumption choices are influenced by their desire to maintain or enhance their social identity by aligning with a group that reflects their values and status. Furthermore, CSR actions in the luxury sector come into focus revealing a significant relationship with consumers' willingness to pay premium prices for luxury products (Diallo et al. 2021). We found CSR a significant theme across the timeframe (Figure  8). It encompasses a wide range of practices designed to meet the expectations of diverse stakeholders. Luxury brands like Prada, LVMH, and ITC publish detailed sections in their annual reports on CSR initiatives on sustainability. Based on the premise that CSR enhances consumer perception and preference of luxury brands, it becomes critical to identify which CSR initiatives by luxury firms garner consumer favour, assessing varying appeal across luxury consumer segments. Another key takeaway is that a carefully implemented, employee-focused CSR can improve financial performance and customer loyalty for luxury companies, while poorly executed CSR can have the opposite effect (Sipilä et al. 2021). This happens because thoughtful CSR initiatives build genuine consumer trust and loyalty, while poorly executed efforts raise scepticism and reduce brand value. A key factor is the understanding of sustainability within luxury with millennials exhibiting greater sensitivity across cultures (Kapferer and Michaut-Denizeau  2020). The study on green-luxury cars adds depth, highlighting the moderation effects of materialism and cultural values on the relationship between status motivation and purchase intention (Ali et al. 2019). The mediating role of functional and symbolic value dimensions emphasises the complex nature of ethical considerations in luxury consumption (Diallo et al. 2021). Conversely, the reluctance to embrace recycled materials in luxury goods underscores the prioritisation of intrinsic product quality over ethical considerations in luxury purchases (Achabou and Dekhili 2013). Ethical dimensions and perceived trade-offs will likely vary across individuals, each bearing different self-concepts and environmental consciousness. Also, the investigation into consumers' ethical views in luxury versus commodity purchases reveals a dichotomy, stressing the need for a tailored approach to addressing ethical concerns in the luxury sector (Davies, Lee, and Ahonkhai 2012).

This theme, comprising eight papers, stands apart from other clusters due to its strategic integration of CE within luxury companies. Morea, Fortunati, and Martiniello  (2021) and De Angelis, Adıgüzel, and Amatulli  (2017) highlight the progressive steps taken by these companies to incorporate eco-friendly design, reuse, and responsible production as essential components of their corporate strategies for enhanced environmental sustainability. De Angelis, Adıgüzel, and Amatulli  (2017) posit that luxury brands can be both “gold” and “green.” They examine the role of product design in driving sustainable luxury adoption and suggest that while designing luxury offerings, firms may be better off making them similar in design to their earlier non-green offerings versus designs made by non-green companies. Also, this strategy is likely to work more for brands that are durable (vs. ephemeral) and for consumers who are knowledgeable (De Angelis, Adıgüzel, and Amatulli 2017). The study by Morea, Fortunati, and Martiniello (2021) focuses on how combining CSR with CE can promote sustainability in the luxury sector. They offer a framework for using these strategies together to support ecofriendly business practices. Focus of these studies heightens the importance of corporate strategy in advancing sustainability, revealing how luxury brands can align their strategic initiatives with environmental goals. Janssen et al. (2014) and Janssen, Vanhamme, and Leblanc (2017) share design challenges luxury firms face in being perceived as socially responsible. These studies are an acknowledgement of the growing importance of brand conspicuousness and product design in shaping consumer attitudes towards responsible luxury. Aligning green products with established design aesthetics positively influences consumer perceptions and acceptance. Janssen, Vanhamme, and Leblanc (2017) also advance the understanding of how brand conspicuousness affects consumers' perceptions of CSR in luxury brands. They show that luxury branding strategies influence how a compatible CSR appears with luxury, shaping consumer attitudes based on their personal values and the brand's image. Amatulli et  al.  (2018) explored luxury strategies for green products, indicating that external CSR initiatives (vs. internal), particularly those that are more visible, enhance purchase intentions, especially among consumers who value status and conspicuous consumption. Septianto, Seo, and Errmann  (2021) and Grazzini, Acuti, and Aiello  (2021) explore the role of emotional appeals and social media in promoting sustainable luxury brands. Septianto, Seo, and Errmann  (2021) demonstrate the impact of pride and gratitude on consumer engagement. Specifically, they note that pride appeal positively impacts consumers' intention to engage in eWOM driven by self-attainment motives. Grazzini, Acuti, and Aiello  (2021) studied how sustainable attributes, such as recycled materials, impact consumers' purchase intentions for both luxury and fast fashion products. They identified perceived warmth as a key psychological factor that drives consumers to favour products that are both fashionable and environmentally friendly. These studies highlight the significance of emotional engagement and digital communication strategies in fostering consumer support for sustainable luxury. While there is strong support for effective communication strategies in promoting luxury sustainability, we believe there is scope for greater research in examining the effectiveness of different Integrated Marketing Communication strategies, including framing effects (e.g., centrality of green attributes, conspicuousness, attribution), in promoting sustainability in the luxury industry.

This cluster, comprising seven papers, provides a comprehensive overview from a consumer lens. Turunen, Cervellon, and Carey (2020) explore the redefinition of traditional roles, particularly the emergence of consumers as buyers and sellers of luxury goods. This shift has significant theoretical implications as it suggests a transformation in luxury consumption's traditional economic and social dynamics, where consumers are not just passive buyers but active participants in the market. Selling luxury items alters the symbolic value of products and empowers consumers through the financial transaction process, reshaping social roles and contributing to others perceiving them as a sustainable consumer (Turunen, Cervellon, and Carey 2020). This empowerment can lead to a more dynamic and participatory marketplace, where consumer influence on luxury branding and market trends is more pronounced. A real-world example of this can be seen in platforms like The RealReal, where consumers buy and sell pre-owned luxury goods. This not only extends the lifecycle of luxury items, promoting sustainability, but also allows consumers to engage actively in the luxury market, altering traditional perceptions of luxury ownership. Studies on green fashion and conspicuous consumption of prosocial products highlight the evolving nature of consumer roles (Cervellon and Wernerfelt 2012). The study shows that individuals in green fashion communities are motivated by both wanting to look good and caring about social causes. It highlights how their focus shifts from being sustainable to a deeper understanding of the entire sustainable supply chain (Cervellon and Wernerfelt 2012). Johnson, Tariq, and Baker (2018) demonstrate that pro-social self-concept and consumers' status needs positively impact conspicuous consumption of sustainable offerings. They highlight that consumers may engage in pro-social behaviour to achieve recognition in any desirable group, independent of their association with wealth. While costly signalling is often used as an explanation for engaging in sustainable luxury, Johnson, Tariq, and Baker's  (2018) findings have added this additional dimension. Moraes et  al.  (2017) note that efforts to make fine jewellery more ethical will succeed only if the ethical aspects of these products are deeply integrated into the entire consumer experience, especially within the consumption environment. This integration is essential because consumers' roles in sustainable luxury involve both the material and symbolic dimensions of the product, influenced by social processes and the context of consumption (Moraes et al. 2017). Moreover, the effects of environmental claims on consumer evaluations, reveal that such claims enhance perceptions of utilitarian and luxury products, particularly when emphasising personal-social benefits (Steinhart, Ayalon, and Puterman 2013). A practical illustration of leveraging this consumer shift comes from the brand Patagonia, which appeals to consumers through its commitment to environmental sustainability while also being a status symbol among environmentally conscious consumers. Theoretically, these studies highlight the complex motivations behind consumer behaviour, blending status-seeking with ethical considerations and challenging traditional views of conspicuous consumption as purely status-driven. Summing up our review of sustainable luxury literature thematically, we explore five comprehensive areas: Sustainable Fashion, Green Practices in Hospitality, Sharing Economy in Luxury, Sustainable Strategies, and Consumer Roles in Luxury Buying. These clusters highlight organisational practices, consumer views, ethics, and effective communication associated with luxury products. We next explore avenues for future research in understanding possible opportunities of how sustainable luxury impacts marketing and consumer behaviour.
